At a glance

This lesson covers the eyelids, conjunctiva and lacrimal apparatus, the muscles that move the eyelid and eyeball, and the nerves and vessels of the orbit.

Eyelid and conjunctiva

Structure of the eyelid

From outside inwards the eyelid is formed of four layers. The two tarsi unite at the medial angle of the orbit to form the medial palpebral ligament and at the lateral angle to form the lateral palpebral ligament (raphe).

  1. Skin
  2. Palpebral part of orbicularis oculi
  3. TarsusSuperior in upper lid, inferior in lower lid
  4. Palpebral conjunctivaLines the inner surface of the lids

The conjunctiva

Definition

The conjunctiva is a transparent membrane that lines the eyelids and covers the eyeball.

Bulbar conjunctiva

  • Covers the eyeball
  • Opposite the cornea it is reduced to a single layer

Palpebral conjunctiva

  • Lines the upper and lower eyelids
  • Reflected onto the eyeball to form the superior and inferior fornix

When the eyelids are closed the conjunctiva becomes a completely closed sac.

Lacrimal apparatus

In shortTears pass from the lacrimal gland to the superior fornix, then drain through the puncta, canaliculi, sac and duct into the inferior meatus of the nose.

Drainage pathway

Lacrimal gland
Gland ducts
Conjunctival sac
Puncta and canaliculi
Lacrimal sac
Nasolacrimal duct
Inferior meatus

Components

  • Lacrimal gland: the orbital part is the main part and lies in the lacrimal fossa in the anterolateral part of the orbital roof. The palpebral part lies in the lateral part of the upper eyelid deep to the conjunctiva. Levator palpebrae superioris separates the two parts.
  • Gland ducts: open into the superior fornix of the conjunctiva. Blinking withdraws the tears into the conjunctival sac.
  • Canaliculi and puncta: each is 1 cm long, one in each eyelid. A canaliculus starts at the lacrimal punctum, passes behind the medial palpebral ligament and opens into the lacrimal sac.
  • Lacrimal sac: lies in the lacrimal groove at the anterior end of the medial wall of the orbit.
  • Nasolacrimal duct: passes through the nasolacrimal canal and opens in the inferior meatus of the nose.
High-yield

The nasolacrimal duct opening is guarded by a mucous membrane fold, Hasner's valve, which prevents air from the nose entering the lacrimal sac.

Nerve supply of the lacrimal gland

  • Sensory: lacrimal nerve, a branch of the ophthalmic nerve.
  • Sympathetic: from the plexus around the ophthalmic artery.
  • Parasympathetic: preganglionic fibers arise from the lacrimatory part of the superior salivary nucleus in the pons.

Parasympathetic pathway

Superior salivary nucleus (pons)
Facial nerve
Greater petrosal nerve
Sphenopalatine ganglion (relay)
Zygomatic nerve
Zygomatico-temporal nerve
Lacrimal nerve

The postganglionic fibers leave the sphenopalatine ganglion with the zygomatic nerve and its zygomatico-temporal branch (a branch of the maxillary nerve). A twig from the zygomatico-temporal nerve joins the lacrimal nerve, which carries these fibers to the gland.

Extraocular muscles

In shortLevator palpebrae superioris lifts the upper lid; four recti and two obliques move the eyeball.

The four recti arise from the common annular ring that surrounds the optic canal, with part from the superior orbital fissure. Each rectus is inserted into the sclera at a different distance from the limbus (the corneoscleral junction).

MuscleOriginInsertionNerve supplyAction
Levator palpebrae superiorisRoof of orbit just above the optic canalThree slips: skin of upper eyelid, superior tarsus, superior fornix of conjunctivaSuperior division of oculomotor and sympathetic fibersElevates upper eyelid; opens superior fornix to promote flow of tears
Superior rectusCommon annular ringSclera 7.5 mm above limbusSuperior division of oculomotorRotates cornea superiomedially
Inferior rectusCommon annular ringSclera 6.5 mm below limbusInferior division of oculomotorRotates cornea inferiomedially
Medial rectusCommon annular ringSclera 5.5 mm medial to limbusInferior division of oculomotorRotates cornea medially
Lateral rectusCommon annular ringSclera 6.9 mm lateral to limbusAbducent nerveRotates cornea laterally
Superior obliqueRoof of orbit just in front of the optic canalPosterolateral superior quadrant of eyeball, after hooking on the trochleaTrochlear nerveRotates cornea inferio-laterally
Inferior obliqueAnteromedial part of floor of orbitPosterolateral inferior quadrant of eyeball, passing below the eyeballInferior division of oculomotorRotates cornea superio-laterally
High-yield

Lateral rectus is supplied by the abducent nerve and superior oblique by the trochlear nerve. All the other muscles of this group are supplied by the oculomotor nerve.

Course of the superior oblique

The tendon passes forwards at the junction of the roof and medial wall of the orbit. At the anterior margin of the orbit it hooks on the trochlea, a small bony process on the anteromedial margin of the orbital roof, then passes backwards and laterally to its insertion.

Motor nerves of the orbit

Oculomotor (III)

  • Arises from the oculomotor nucleus and Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the midbrain
  • Emerges from the medial side of the cerebral peduncle in the interpeduncular fossa
  • Runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus above the trochlear nerve
  • Divides at the anterior end of the sinus; both divisions enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure inside the common tendinous ring

Trochlear (IV)

  • Arises from the trochlear nucleus in the midbrain
  • Emerges from the lateral side of the cerebral peduncle; the only cranial nerve to emerge from the back of the brainstem
  • Runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus below the oculomotor and above the ophthalmic nerve
  • Enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure outside the common tendinous ring

Abducent (VI)

  • Arises from the abducent nucleus in the pons
  • Emerges from the groove between the pons and the pyramid of the medulla
  • Runs in the floor of the cavernous sinus inferolateral to the internal carotid artery
  • Enters the orbit through the lower part of the superior orbital fissure inside the common tendinous ring

Branches of the oculomotor nerve

Superior division
Levator palpebrae superioris, superior rectus
Inferior division
Medial rectus, inferior rectus, inferior oblique
Parasympathetic fibers
Ciliary muscle and sphincter pupillae (preganglionic)

Ophthalmic nerve (sensory supply)

The ophthalmic nerve is the smallest division of the trigeminal nerve. It passes in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus between the trochlear and maxillary nerves. At the anterior end of the sinus it divides into three branches that enter the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.

Ophthalmic nerve
  • Frontal
    • Supratrochlear
    • Supraorbital
  • Lacrimal
  • Nasociliary
    • Ganglionic branches two
    • Long ciliary
    • Posterior ethmoidal
    • Anterior ethmoidal
    • Infratrochlear

Frontal nerve

  • Enters the orbit outside the common tendinous ring and passes forwards below the roof, above levator palpebrae superioris. It is the most superior structure in the orbit.
  • About the middle of the roof it divides into the supratrochlear and supraorbital nerves.
  • Supratrochlear: skin of the medial part of the upper eyelid and the lower part of the forehead.
  • Supraorbital: skin of the upper eyelid, forehead and scalp as far as the lambdoid suture.

Lacrimal nerve

Enters outside the common tendinous ring, then passes laterally on the upper border of lateral rectus to the anterolateral end of the orbit. It supplies the lateral part of the upper eyelid and the lacrimal gland.

Nasociliary nerve

Enters the orbit within the common tendinous ring between the two divisions of the oculomotor nerve, then runs along the medial wall between medial rectus and superior oblique.

Two ganglionic branches
Suspend the nasociliary ganglion
Long ciliary nerves
Sensory to the eyeball
Posterior ethmoidal
Posterior ethmoidal and sphenoidal air sinuses (through the posterior ethmoidal foramen)
Anterior ethmoidal
Ethmoidal air sinuses, anterior cranial fossa, nasal cavity, skin of lower half of nose
Infratrochlear
Skin of medial part of both eyelids, their conjunctiva, skin of upper half of nose

The anterior ethmoidal nerve passes through the anterior ethmoidal foramen into the anterior cranial fossa. It enters the nose through the cribriform plate as the internal nasal nerve, then reaches the face as the external nasal nerve.

Entry through the superior orbital fissure

Inside the common tendinous ring

  • Superior and inferior divisions of the oculomotor nerve
  • Nasociliary nerve (between the two oculomotor divisions)
  • Abducent nerve

Outside the common tendinous ring

  • Trochlear nerve
  • Frontal nerve
  • Lacrimal nerve

Nasociliary ganglion

A small parasympathetic ganglion in the orbital fat above and lateral to the optic nerve, suspended by the nasociliary nerve. It has three roots.

RootOriginRelay in ganglionSupplies
SensoryTwo ganglionic branches from the nasociliary nerveNoAll parts of the eyeball (sensory)
SympatheticPostganglionic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion, via the plexus around the ophthalmic arteryNoDilator pupillae and blood vessels of the eyeball
ParasympatheticPreganglionic fibers from the Edinger-Westphal part of the oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain, via the inferior division of the oculomotor and the nerve to inferior obliqueYesSphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle (postganglionic fibers)
Don't confuse

Only the parasympathetic root relays in the nasociliary ganglion. The sensory and sympathetic fibers pass through without relay.

Blood supply of the orbit

Ophthalmic artery

  • A branch of the internal carotid artery just after it emerges from the cavernous sinus.
  • Enters the orbit through the optic canal below the optic nerve.
  • Passes forwards on the medial wall of the orbit, accompanied by the nasociliary nerve.

Its branches are:

  1. Central artery of the retina
  2. Lacrimal branch to the lacrimal gland
  3. Ciliary branches to the eyeball
  4. Muscular branches to the orbital muscles
  5. Posterior ethmoidal artery (with the posterior ethmoidal nerve)
  6. Anterior ethmoidal artery (with the anterior ethmoidal nerve)
  7. Dorsal nasal
  8. Supraorbital
  9. Medial palpebral branch
  10. Supratrochlear
Clinical relevance

The central artery of the retina arises below the optic nerve. It is small but very important: its occlusion leads to blindness.

Veins of the orbit

Superior ophthalmic vein
Communicates with the anterior facial vein
Inferior ophthalmic vein
Communicates with the pterygoid venous plexus through small veins passing through the inferior orbital fissure
Both ophthalmic veins
End in the cavernous sinus; considered long emissary veins

Key terms

Check yourself

Which muscle is supplied by the trochlear nerve?

The superior oblique.

Which nerves enter the orbit outside the common tendinous ring?

The trochlear, frontal and lacrimal nerves.

Which root of the nasociliary ganglion relays in the ganglion?

The parasympathetic root, from the Edinger-Westphal part of the oculomotor nucleus.

Where do the postganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal gland arise?

In the sphenopalatine ganglion; they pass with the zygomatic nerve and its zygomatico-temporal branch.

Key Points / Quick Review

Eyelid and conjunctiva

  • Eyelid layers from outside: skin, palpebral orbicularis oculi, tarsus, palpebral conjunctiva.
  • Bulbar conjunctiva covers the eyeball; palpebral conjunctiva lines the lids; they meet at the superior and inferior fornix.

Lacrimal apparatus

  • Gland (orbital and palpebral parts), ducts, canaliculi with puncta, sac, nasolacrimal duct.
  • Duct opens in the inferior meatus; Hasner's valve prevents air entering the sac.
  • Parasympathetic relay is in the sphenopalatine ganglion.

Muscles

  • Levator palpebrae superioris: superior division of oculomotor plus sympathetic fibers.
  • Superior rectus: superior division of oculomotor; medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique: inferior division.
  • Lateral rectus: abducent; superior oblique: trochlear.
  • Rectus insertions: superior 7.5 mm, lateral 6.9 mm, inferior 6.5 mm, medial 5.5 mm from the limbus.

Nerves

  • Oculomotor, nasociliary and abducent enter inside the tendinous ring; trochlear, frontal and lacrimal enter outside it.
  • Trochlear is the only cranial nerve emerging from the back of the brainstem.
  • Ophthalmic nerve branches: frontal, lacrimal, nasociliary.

Nasociliary ganglion

  • Three roots: sensory and sympathetic pass without relay; parasympathetic relays.
  • Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers supply sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle.

Vessels

  • Ophthalmic artery enters through the optic canal below the optic nerve.
  • Occlusion of the central artery of the retina leads to blindness.
  • Ophthalmic veins end in the cavernous sinus.
